title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features
authors: Andrew Ilyas, Shibani Santurkar, Dimitris Tsipras, Logan Engstrom, Brandon Tran, Aleksander Madry

pages.title: The puzzle of adversarial examples
pages.subtitle: A tiny, imperceptible nudge flips the prediction

blocks.html: The point of this page: modern image classifiers can be fooled by perturbations so small a human cannot see them — add a faint, invisible pattern to a photo of a pig and the network confidently says “airplane.” For years this was treated as a bug: evidence the models were broken or brittle. This paper argues it is the opposite — a feature.

Shared vocabulary (recurring across this collection). An adversarial example is an input nudged by a tiny perturbation $\delta$ that flips the prediction while looking unchanged to us; the change is bounded by a norm — the $\ell_2$ norm caps the total length of $\delta$, the $\ell_\infty$ norm caps each pixel's change — inside an $\epsilon$-ball around the clean input. This paper asks why those examples exist at all, not how to make or defeat them.

The startling claim. Adversarial examples are not flukes. They are a direct consequence of the model doing exactly what we trained it to do: extract every scrap of signal that predicts the label. Some of that signal lives in patterns that are real and predictive but imperceptible to humans. The authors call these non-robust features, and adversarial examples are simply the act of toggling them.
Adversarial vulnerability is a direct result of sensitivity to well-generalizing features in the data.

Why the reframing matters. It changes what a “fix” looks like. If adversarial examples were noise, better optimization or more data might erase them. But if they come from real predictive structure, robustness requires us to choose to ignore that structure — which can cost accuracy. This is the paper's bridge from the attack/defense papers (FGSM, C&W, PGD) to a theory of why the whole phenomenon exists.

The intuition. A feature here is any function $f$ of the input whose value correlates with the label. The whole paper hinges on splitting features into two camps by how they behave under a small adversarial perturbation: ones that survive it (robust) and ones a tiny nudge can flip (non-robust).

A concrete example. Think of classifying cats vs. dogs. A robust feature is something like “has pointy triangular ears” — a human uses it too, and you'd have to change the image a lot to destroy it. A non-robust feature might be a faint texture-statistics pattern, invisible to you, that happens to correlate with “cat” across the dataset — genuinely predictive, but an $\epsilon$-sized nudge can flip its sign so it now votes “dog.” Both lower training loss, so a standard classifier uses both.
Formal definition 1 — a useful feature. A feature $f$ (normalized to mean 0, variance 1) is $\rho$-useful if it is correlated with the label by at least $\rho$ on average:

Term by term: $(x,y)$ is an example and its label (taken as $\pm 1$ for a two-class sketch); $f(x)$ is the feature's value; the product $y\cdot f(x)$ is positive when the feature agrees with the label; $\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}$ averages over the data distribution $\mathcal{D}$; and $\rho \ge 0$ is how strongly it agrees on average. Larger $\rho$ = more useful for prediction.
Formal definition 2 — a robustly useful feature. A feature is $\gamma$-robustly useful if it stays useful even after an adversary perturbs the input within the $\epsilon$-ball:

Term by term: the inner $\inf_{\|\delta\|\le\epsilon}$ is the adversary, picking the worst perturbation $\delta$ of size at most $\epsilon$ to make the feature disagree with the label; $f(x+\delta)$ is the feature on the attacked input; we then average that worst case over the data. If it still beats $\gamma > 0$, the feature is robust — no small nudge can turn it against the label.

The dangerous middle case. A non-robust feature is $\rho$-useful for some $\rho > 0$ (helps on clean data) but is not robustly useful — the worst-case term above is negative, so a tiny $\delta$ flips its vote. These are exactly the features an adversary exploits.

items: Robust features: edges, shapes, large textures — what a human relies on; hard to destroy with a small nudge.
Non-robust features: faint statistical patterns, invisible to us, genuinely correlated with the label, but easily flipped by an imperceptible perturbation.
Standard training has no reason to prefer one over the other — it greedily uses both because both lower the loss.

pages.title: Why standard training drinks the poison
pages.subtitle: Accuracy and robustness can genuinely conflict

blocks.html: The setup. Suppose a non-robust feature agrees with the label 95% of the time. A loss-minimizing classifier should use it — it lowers test error. The model is not being stupid; it is being accurate. The catch is that the same feature is, by definition, trivial for an adversary to flip.

Standard classification, formally. Ordinary training minimizes expected loss, which leads the model to lean on the full set of useful features — robust and non-robust. Robust training instead minimizes the worst-case loss inside the $\epsilon$-ball (the saddle-point objective from the PGD/Madry paper), which forces the model to rely on robustly-useful features only:

Term by term: $L(\theta,x,y)$ is the loss of the network with weights $\theta$; the standard objective averages it; the robust objective inserts an inner $\max_{\|\delta\|\le\epsilon}$ — the adversary — before averaging. The inner max is precisely what blinds the model to features a small $\delta$ can flip, i.e. the non-robust ones.

The famous tension explained. Robust models often have lower clean accuracy than standard models. This is not a training failure — the robust model is deliberately throwing away real, useful (non-robust) signal in exchange for stability. The accuracy–robustness trade-off is baked into the data, not the algorithm.
Human perception relies only on robust features ... the standard classifier uses any available signal, even features incomprehensible to humans.
Why it matters. This reframes robustness as a choice about which features are allowed, and explains the trade-off that earlier work (PGD/Madry) observed empirically but did not fully account for.

pages.title: Experiment 1: a robust dataset
pages.subtitle: Strip out the non-robust features, and robustness transfers

blocks.html: The hypothesis to test. If adversarial vulnerability really comes from non-robust features in the data, then we should be able to build a dataset that contains only robust features, train a perfectly ordinary classifier on it, and get a robust model for free — with no adversarial training at the final step. If robustness transfers through the data, the features story is right.

items: Start with a model that was already adversarially trained, so its learned representation depends on robust features only.
For each clean image $x$, optimize a new image $x_R$ so that its deep representation (the penultimate-layer activations) matches $x$'s, as seen through this robust model: $g(x_R) \approx g(x)$.

The result is a “robustified” image: it looks roughly like the original to a human, but its non-robust features have been scrubbed away (the robust model couldn't see them, so matching its representation doesn't preserve them).
Train a brand-new classifier on this robust dataset using completely standard (non-adversarial) training.

blocks.tex: x_R = \arg\min_{x'}\; \big\| g(x') - g(x) \big\|_2 \quad\text{($g$ = features of a robust model)}

blocks.html: Term by term: $g(\cdot)$ is the representation (activations) of the pretrained robust model; $g(x)$ is the target representation of the original image; we search for an image $x'$ whose representation matches it, starting the optimization from a different image so non-robust artifacts of $x$ aren't copied. The minimizer $x_R$ keeps the robust content and drops the rest.

The payoff. A classifier trained normally on this robust dataset is substantially robust to adversarial attacks — far more than a normally-trained model on the original data. Robustness came from the data, not the training algorithm. Strong evidence that the vulnerability lived in the features all along.

pages.title: Experiment 2: a non-robust dataset
pages.subtitle: Mislabeled by a perturbation, yet it generalizes

blocks.html: The knockout punch. The authors build a dataset that is completely mislabeled from a human's point of view — the pictures look like one thing but are labeled another — and yet a model trained on it generalizes well on the normal, clean test set. If human-nonsense labels still teach a model to classify real images, the labels must align with something real the model can see: non-robust features.

items: Take a correctly labeled image — say, a dog (true label “dog”).
Pick a target label, e.g. “cat,” and apply a small adversarial perturbation that makes a standard classifier call the dog a cat.
Relabel the perturbed image as “cat” and add it to the new dataset — the image still looks like a dog to you, but its label now says cat.
Do this for every image, so the dataset's labels are systematically “wrong” to a human.

blocks.html: The result. A model trained only on these human-wrong labels learns to classify real, clean test images correctly. How? The adversarial perturbation injected non-robust features pointing at the new (cat) label, and those non-robust features are genuinely predictive on natural data. The model latched onto exactly the imperceptible signal the perturbation planted — signal that, on clean test cats, really does indicate “cat.”
Models can learn from human-meaningless features alone and still generalize well to the standard test set.

Why this settles it. If non-robust features were noise, training on them could only memorize, never generalize. Generalization to clean images proves they carry real predictive power. Adversarial examples are simply the act of toggling those features — not a bug, a feature.

pages.title: What this changes
pages.subtitle: A human-centric, not model-centric, view of robustness

blocks.html: The relocation. Adversarial examples are reframed as a human–machine misalignment: the model uses predictive features humans never evolved to perceive, and the adversary exploits the gap. The flaw is not in any one model or training method — it is a property of the dataset and of the mismatch between what humans and networks find informative.

items: Robustness is a choice, not a patch: we impose it by restricting which features a model may use, accepting the cost.
The accuracy–robustness trade-off is fundamental: robust training deliberately discards useful (non-robust) signal, so some clean accuracy is genuinely lost.

Transferability is explained: different models trained on the same data pick up the same non-robust features, so an attack crafted on one transfers to another — the empirical fact FGSM first reported now has a mechanism.

Interpretability improves with robust models: because they rely on robust features, their input gradients align with human-perceptible structure — the saliency-map observation from the PGD/Madry paper.

blocks.html: The lasting message. If we want models that “see” like we do, we must train them to rely only on features we consider meaningful — and accept that this may cost raw accuracy. Adversarial vulnerability is, in this view, the price of using all the signal the data offers.

How it connects. FGSM showed adversarial examples follow a predictable direction; C&W and PGD made the attacks strong and the defenses real; obfuscated gradients policed how we measure them. This paper supplies the explanation underneath all of it: the direction FGSM found, the features PGD's robust models learned to ignore, and the transfer everyone observed are all the same thing — non-robust features in the data.
